problem_summary.summary: Return the number of nodes on the longest root-to-leaf path, or zero for an empty tree.
problem_summary.input_output: Input: the root of a binary tree. Return its maximum depth as an integer.

brute_force.explanation: For every node, independently traverse its subtree to measure its height, then return the largest height found. Re-traversal makes this a deliberately simple but slower baseline.
brute_force.correctness_idea: The root is among the visited nodes, and its measured height is the maximum depth of the whole tree. Taking the maximum over all subtree heights therefore includes the correct answer.
brute_force.time_complexity: O(n^2) worst case for a skewed tree, because subtree heights are recomputed at each node.
brute_force.space_complexity: O(n) auxiliary for the node list and explicit traversal stack; no call-stack depth risk.

optimized.explanation: Use breadth-first traversal and count levels. Each queue layer corresponds to one additional node on every root-to-node path reaching that level.
optimized.correctness_idea: BFS visits nodes in nondecreasing depth. Counting each complete level counts exactly the number of nodes on the deepest root-to-leaf path.
optimized.time_complexity: O(n) — each node is enqueued and removed once.
optimized.space_complexity: O(w) auxiliary for the queue, where w is the maximum number of nodes at any level.

steps.action: Visit 8 and enqueue its children 3 and 10.

steps.condition: The two nodes currently queued form one complete level.
steps.action: Visit 3 and 10; enqueue 6 from 3 and 14 from 10.
Visit 6 and 14; no children are added.

edge_cases.handling: The optimized method returns zero before starting BFS.
The root is one level, so the returned depth is one.
BFS counts every level; its queue remains small even when the height is n.
